This constitutes a cautiously favorable stance.

report:
**Conclusion: Probably true, but not proven as a stand-alone causal effect.** Higher olive-oil intake is consistently associated with fewer strokes, especially in Mediterranean-diet populations. A meta-analysis including studies of 38,673 people for stroke found an inverse association, though much of this evidence was observational and can be influenced by other healthy dietary and lifestyle habits. [https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-of-nutrition/article/olive-oil-consumption-and-risk-of-chd-andor-stroke-a-metaanalysis-of-casecontrol-cohort-and-intervention-studies/79A90337470271D8A8CE2FDC77BD869E](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-of-nutrition/article/olive-oil-consumption-and-risk-of-chd-andor-stroke-a-metaanalysis-of-casecontrol-cohort-and-intervention-studies/79A90337470271D8A8CE2FDC77BD869E)

A prospective study in older adults likewise specifically examined olive-oil intake and incident stroke and reported lower stroke incidence with higher consumption/oleic-acid levels. [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21676914/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21676914/)

The strongest causal evidence is indirect: in PREDIMED, people at high cardiovascular risk assigned to a Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil had fewer *major cardiovascular events* (a composite including stroke) than those assigned to a lower-fat control diet. That tests an olive-oil–enriched dietary pattern, not simply adding olive oil to an otherwise unchanged diet. [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29897866/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29897866/)

Thus, using olive oil—particularly extra-virgin olive oil—to replace saturated fats within an overall Mediterranean-style diet is a reasonable stroke-risk–reducing choice. Evidence does not establish that adding olive oil alone, without beneficial substitutions or broader dietary changes, will reduce stroke risk.
